title: Parameter Updates During Calibration Process
text:
Manual Adjustments
Between automated calibration runs, targeted manual adjustments were made to improve emergent ecosystem dynamics. These included:

1. Maturation Ogives
Maturation ogives were modified to prevent unrealistic population growth in species using a “recruits-per-adult” reproduction option. In particular, reproduction was disabled for the first age class to avoid numerical instabilities caused by exponential recruitment feedback.


2. Benthic Species Spatial Distribution
Benthic species spatial distribution was corrected by activating a model flag that enforces habitat mapping based on input data, ensuring consistency with spatial constraints.


3. Predation Mortality Rates
Predation mortality rates (mQ) were initially set to zero for all groups, except juvenile stages of age-structured species, for which mQ remained active to prevent uncontrolled demographic expansion during calibration.


4. Starvation Mortality Responses
Starvation mortality responses were enhanced by increasing the sensitivity to food limitation:

Kthreshm was increased (from X to X)
mStrav was also raised (from X to X)
flag_shrink parameter was set to 1, enabling individuals to lose structural or reserve biomass under starvation conditions

title: Parametrization of the Contaminant Submodule for PCBs
text:
Implementation

Uptake and Transfer

Uptake activation: Uptake was activated for zooplankton, enabling trophic transfer and bioaccumulation throughout the food web
Tracking: Accumulation and transfer were explicitly tracked for each congener
Maternal transfer: Maternal transfer of contaminants was enabled in Atlantis and implemented for this case study



Biological Effects
Effects on growth, mortality, and reproduction were based on the equations presented in Lovindeer et al. (2025):

Reproductive effects: Generalized to allow for two additional response shapes using the same functional form as for growth
Parameterization: Lethal and sublethal responses were parameterized using a meta-analysis of contaminant impact studies
Application: Biological effects were applied based on the total PCB body concentration



Concentration Estimation
A conversion factor was applied to estimate total PCB concentrations from individual congener levels.

title: Atlantis Model for Puget Sound
text:
This website records changes to the Atlantis Model for Puget Sound (AMPS) from the original published model described in the Technical memorandum
Morzaria-Luna H, Kaplan IC, Harvey CJ, Girardin R, Fulton EA, MacCready P, Chasco B, Horne P, Schmidt M. 2022. Design and Parameterization of a Spatially Explicit Atlantis Ecosystem Model for Puget Sound. Northwest Fisheries Science Center (U.S.). NOAA technical memorandum NMFS-NWFSC 177. DOI : https://doi.org/10.25923/tnp6-mf67
The model was built using the Atlantis modeling framework, a simulation modeling approach developed by Dr. Beth Fulton at the Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation (CSIRO) (Weijerman2016?). Atlantis integrates physical, chemical, ecological, and anthropogenic processes in a three-dimensional, spatially explicit domain. This framework has been applied to evaluate management scenarios and investigate the effects of climate change in over 30 ecosystems worldwide. In Atlantis, ecosystem dynamics are represented by spatially explicit submodels that simulate oceanographic processes, biogeochemical factors driving primary production, and food web relations among flora and fauna. The model represents species of ecological and conservation concern and key exploited species at the level of detail necessary to evaluate the direct effects of fishing, and it represents other anthropogenic and climate impacts on the ecosystem as a whole.
Our aim is to leverage and improve the AMPS to focus on broader ecological questions within the zooplankton and fish communities.

title: Atlantis Model for Puget Sound
text:
Atlantis Model for Puget Sound
The Atlantis Model of Puget Sound (AMPS) was developed as part of the Salish Sea Marine Survival Project, a collaboration of 60+ partner organizations focused on declining survival of Chinook and coho salmon. The model was designed to test both bottom-up effects on salmon (e.g. changes in primary production, zooplankton community structure, and availability and timing of forage fish and other prey) and top-down effects (e.g. predation by pinnipeds on juvenile salmon). The model simulates ecological and food web dynamics of four zooplankton functional groups (i.e. aggregates of similar species), twelve other invertebrate groups, four primary producers, benthic and pelagic bacteria, three detrital categories, and 48 vertebrate groups, including fish, marine mammals, sharks and birds. Model development required extensive synthesis of local data contributed by collaborators from NOAA, University of Washington, state and tribal agencies, and others.

title: Atlantis Model for Puget Sound
text:
Geographic extent
The AMPS has 89 polygons that extend over 9652 km2, including 60 water column polygons, 29 islands, and two non-dynamic boundary polygons in the north (Strait of Georgia) and west (Strait of San Juan de Fuca). All model polygons are further divided into water column depth layers, ranging from one layer for nearshore boxes to six for offshore boxes and one sediment layer. Individual polygons within the domain were defined from a combination of geographic features, bathymetry, circulation patterns, ecological characteristics, and, to some extent, management and statistical reporting areas for key state-managed fisheries.

Spatial distributions based on SRKW sightings. Estimated based on Thorson et al. 2015
Seasonal distribution

We updated spatial distribution based on orca master data of killer whale sightings for the years 2011 - 2020. Laura Kohen (NOAA-Western Regional Center, Protected Species Division) carried out the following analysis: To match sightings of Southern Resident killer whales to Puget Sound Atlantis boxes. First, sightings are filtered to only sightings where there was confidence that the sighting was of Southern Resident killer whales (vs other killer whale populations). Specifically, data is filtered to sightings where the “likely pod” is either SRKW, SRs, J, K, or L; so excludes any sightings where the sighting could only be identified to the “orca” level (not more specific). Also excludes sightings that were specified as transients, Northern residents, “not orcas”, or HBs (humpbacks). Data was then filtered to years 2011-2020. From there, we filtered down to unique day-quadrant sightings. Specifically, if there are any 2+ sightings with the same date and Whale Museum specified quadrant number, we only keep 1 sighting with that day-quadrant combo. This is to remove sightings from multiple sources that can inflate occurrence in an area. Note, this then means that there could be multiple sightings on the same day in the same Atlantis box, but they will all be in different Whale Museum quadrants.
Note also that data was filtered down to only sightings with a whale museum identified quadrant number because these will occur in the Salish sea. Note that Whale Museum quadrant extend passed the Atlantis box domain (we do not have a shapefile of the quadrants but image is included with data). This may miss a few sightings if a quadrant was not specified by the Whale Museum but not a large amount.
With the sightings data, sightings were converted to an sf object with latitude and longitude. Then, based on the CRS of the Atlantis polygons, the SRKW sightings sf were projected to the same CRS as the Atlantis polygons so that all are in the same sf space/same traget coordinate reference system (function st_transform). Then using st_intersection, this function finds the Atlantis polygons that each sighting falls into.
The final output file has for all the day-quadrant unique SRKW sightings from 2011-2020, the date (including month, day, year) and the Atlantis polygon where the sighting fell.

Fecundity. Fishery Management Council Working Group, data from Eric Ward, https://nwfsc-cb.github.io/srkw-status/.

title: Responses to temperature and oxygen
text:
Literature Review Methodology
We obtained the parameters for functional group responses to temperature and oxygen by conducting a literature review. The quantity and quality of the information available on sensitivity to temperature and oxygen was highly variable between species. For some species, more than one source was available for some parameters. Where no information was available for a species, we used information from related taxa.
Larvae and eggs are not explicitly represented in Atlantis, and there is no ontogenetic separation for most biological parameters that define functional responses to environmental drivers. Therefore, parameter values for adults were preferred where available. Where information from Puget Sound or the Salish Sea was not available, sources from other geographic regions were used instead, with preference for studies from neighboring geographic regions (e.g., US Pacific Northwest, US West Coast, or Alaska).

Scoring System
Where multiple studies were found for a parameter for a species, we used a scoring rubric to select between parameter values. When scoring a study, we consider the following factors hierarchically: study type, species, life stage, and geographic location. We considered study type to be the most important factor contributing to the score of a parameter because thermal tolerance thresholds can assume different meanings depending on the methodology and aims of a study.
Single-species values were averaged to obtain parameter values for multispecies functional groups.

title: Responses to temperature and oxygen
text:
Temperature

Thermal Tolerance Niches
We imposed restriction to the spatial distributions of functional groups in the model by setting values of minimum and maximum tolerated temperature (parameters min_move_temp and max_move_temp in Atlantis). For many species in the model, particularly for Pacific salmon, we could find several observational studies that linked the presence of a species with the temperatures observed in the field. However, the tolerance limits in Atlantis were intended to be a broad range of temperatures at which a species could occur. As such, we preferred using the broad thermal envelope identified for each species by AquaMaps (Kaschner et al. 2019). AquaMaps (www.aquamaps.org) is a public global database of model-based, large-scale predictions of species occurrences that provides information on species environmental envelopes, including their preferred thermal range.
To capture the effect of temperature on the reproduction of stenothermic species, we parameterized spawning limitations based on the available information on thermal limits for spawning, egg hatching, and larval survival. In Atlantis, the user can define the maximum and minimum values of temperature that allow spawning to occur (parameters min_spawn_temp and max_spawn_temp). These parameters work by preventing the spawning process from occurring if temperature in a cell is outside the defined range, meaning that effects of temperature on eggs or larvae are implicit. Eggs and larvae are not explicitly represented in Atlantis, and it is therefore impossible to distinguish between the effects of temperature on different pre-recruitment stages.


Bioenergetic Responses to Temperature

Consumption
Atlantis allows to represent bioenergetic responses to temperature for ectotherms. We applied a dome-shaped bioenergetic response of ectotherm metabolism to increasing temperature. The response curve follows the formulation of Kitchell et al. (1977) and is applied sensu Rovellini et al. (2024). Briefly, a temperature-dependent correction factor for metabolism \(T_{corr}\) is calculated as:
\[T_{corr} = \frac{V^X \cdot e^{X(1-V)}}{(e^{X})^{0.98(1-V)}}\]
Where:
\[V = \frac{T_{CM} - T}{T_{CM} - T_{C0}}\]
\[X = \frac{(ln(Q_{10})(T_{CM} - T_{C0} + 2))^2}{400}\]
Where \(T_{C0}\) is the temperature of highest consumption, \(T_{CM}\) is the water temperature above which no consumption occurs, and \(Q_{10}\) approximates the slope of the ascending limb of the curve. In Atlantis, the multiplier gets applied to consumption-dependent growth (parameters mum and C), and also to the mortality terms (mL and mQ).


Respiration
Atlantis allows to represent maintenance costs via implicit assimilation efficiency and, for age-structured groups, by modeling temperature- and weight-dependent respiration explicitly. We turned on respiration, as this feature was turned off in the original version of the model. Then, we imposed an effect of temperature on fish respiration R (the daily N weight lost to respiration) as:
\[R = K_A \cdot W^{K_B} \cdot e^{K_{tmp} \cdot T}\]
Where \(K_A\) is the allometric respiration constant (mg N mg⁻¹ N d⁻¹), \(W\) is the individual’s dry weight in mg N, \(K_B\) is the allometric respiration exponent, and \(K_{tmp}\) is a constant. Parameters \(K_A\) and \(K_B\) were specific for each functional group, while \(K_{tmp}\) is written in Atlantis to have one value for all teleosts and one for all chondrichthyans (0.086 and 0.075, respectively).
Notably, respiration costs in Atlantis are represented as consumed dry weight, instead of oxygen. This also meant that the units of most of the parameter values obtained from the literature had to be converted accordingly.

Marine Mammal Respiration
For marine mammals, we express the respiration as a function of weight W only, assuming that water temperature does not impact the metabolism rate for endotherm species. Similarly, we assume that bird respiration rates are not a function of the water temperature. For these groups, the respiration is expressed as follows:
\[R = K_A \cdot W^{K_B}\]
where \(K_A\) is the allometric respiration constant (g N·mg⁻¹ N·d⁻¹), \(W\) is the individual’s dry weight in mg N, \(K_B\) is the allometric respiration exponent, and \(K_{tmp}\) is a constant. Parameters \(K_A\) and \(K_B\) were specific for each functional group.

title: Responses to temperature and oxygen
text:
Oxygen Sensitivity
Water-breathing organisms are limited by the concentration of dissolved oxygen available in the water. While oxygen consumption, and therefore susceptibility to oxygen limitation, varies dynamically with body weight and temperature in ectotherms, oxygen concentration is not explicitly included in the current formulation of respiration and bioenergetic responses in Atlantis.
However, to capture the lethal effects of anoxic conditions, which are known to occur in Puget Sound, we imposed lower limits of dissolved oxygen below which mortality occurs (Atlantis parameters XXX_min_O2 for age-structured groups, and KO2LIM_XXX for biomass pools). Parameter values were obtained from the R package published at https://github.com/tessington/metabolic_index (Essington et al., in prep.). We used the predicted posterior medians of the critical oxygen partial pressure for each taxon, converted from kPa to mg m⁻³ using the R package “respR”.

title: Addition of a jellyfish functional group
section: Addition of a Jellyfish functional group
text:
Addition of a Jellyfish functional group

The model simulates food web dynamics using 73 biological groups, including one gelatinous zooplankton. While much effort centered on characterizing pelagic fish abundance, diets, and distribution during the development of the AMPS, data on these attributes are scarcer for jellyfish in Puget Sound. We use data from field studies, mesocosms, and relevant global literature to add a new functional group, based on the jellyfish Aurelia. We incorporate information on total consumption rates of Aurelia on their prey and composition of Aurelia diet.
As part of a WA Sea Grant project, led by Julie Kiester (University of Washington), “Ecosystem impacts of the jellyfish Aurelia labiata in Puget Sound”, we will quantify the ecosystem effects of changing jellyfish populations in Puget Sound. We will examine scenarios that integrate results from mesocosms and field studies part of this grant to understand the ecological role of jellyfish in Puget Sound, and their effects on other species including salmon and forage fish. Spatial representation in the Atlantis Model for Puget Sound (AMPS) will allow us to test the impact of spatial aggregations of Aurelia identified in aerial monitoring by EOPS, for instance in South Sound inlets. Vertical structure in the model allows us to capture diel vertical movement of jellyfish and other zooplankton taxa, which will be informed by field sampling.
#Current parameterization of ‘Gelatinous zooplankton’
In its initial version, the AMPS included one ‘Gelatinous zooplankton’ functional group, which encompassed scyphozoans, larvaceans, siphonophores, and ctenophores. Other plankton groups, including jellyfish prey, were aggregated into five additional functional groups (Table 1). The composition of the ‘Gelatinous zooplankton’ functional group was based on samples collected throughout Puget Sound in 2011 and 2014-2017 using zooplankton nets. These nets are likely to entirely miss larger medusae, so we added information from extensive surface trawl sampling of larger jellyfish and pelagic fish undertaken in 2011 across all basins of Puget Sound. We interpolated missing data (per polygon) based on the average of all sampled polygons of similar bottom depth (i.e., with the same number of Atlantis depth layers). Total abundance of gelatinous zooplankton (per Atlantis polygon) was then taken as the sum of large and small jellyfish abundance.

Gelatinous zooplankton diets were compiled from multiple sources, focused on Puget Sound when available (Purcell and Grover 1990, Costello and Colin 2002); these are studies from Puget Sound, that described the diet of small hydromedusae such as Aglantha and Obelia. (Schaub2023?) assessed the trophic ecology of Aurelia labiata in the Strait of Georgia using stable isotopes, and found that the diet of Aurelia was dominated particulate organic matter and zooplankton. Larger jellyfish are know to ingest more copepods, euphausiids, and fish eggs and larvae and show a trophic shift with increasing size (Schaub2023?). Currently, diet of gelatinous zooplankton in the AMPS is: 48.3% microzooplankton; 24.7% mesozooplankton (copepods); and 27% other zooplankton including barnacle larvae, appendicularians, and bivalve larvae. As an approximation, rate parameters, specifically growth and clearance rates, were taken from the California Current Atlantis model (Marshall et al. 2017, Kaplan et al. 2017). We combined the diet of larger Aurelia based on gut contents from (Graham2001?) with the diet of gelatinous zooplankton in the model for parameterization of the new jellyfish functional group. Although (Graham2001?) was not carried out in Puget Sound, it is the only study that provides a detailed description of the diet of Aurelia anywhere in the world. We used the diet of Aurelia from (Graham2001?) to parameterize the new jellyfish functional group, and combined it with the diet of gelatinous zooplankton in the model.

title: Addition of a jellyfish functional group
text:
Updated spatial distribution
We used the results from Green et al. who examined interspecific variation in species-specific response of jellyfish adult life stages to environmental variation and anthropogenic influence, and projected future changes in these parameters in Puget Sound. They used results from a field survey to predict the presence of seven jellyfish species across six sub basins in Puget Sound. They modeled the probability of species presence as a function of site-specific parameters (geomorphic type, anthropogenic land use) and observation-specific variables (salinity, temperature, depth). Their presence/absence models indicated strong interspecific variation in the habitat preferences of jellyfish to environmental parameters such as temperature and geomorphic type, as well as varying sensitivity to potential anthropogenic effects on nearshore waters. Aurelia individuals were associated with large and small backwater embayments rather than exposed shorelines, and human development within these embayments was shown to decrease the probability of presence. We used the embayments derived by Green et al. (embayment_unit_revised.shp) and classified additional coastline segments from data collected by The Salmon and Steelhead Habitat Inventory and Assessment Program (SSHIAP) (geomorph_ps_s.shp from Geodatabase SSHIAP_Marine.gdb>Geomorph_PS_S). Geomorphology categories beach, modified, shoreline, bluff, and platform categories were aggregated and reclassified as exposed; all types of delta were assigned to the delta category. We also derived percent used landcover classes at 30 m resolution (szline_GSU_identity_Spj_HUC_NHD_dissolve_DU_sum_LU.shp).
Development classes were based on the NCCOS’ Coastal Change and Analysis Program (C-CAP, 2006 analysis year).
